Start: 15:30 PT
Duration: 62 min
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Mills (Redwood AE), Priya Anand (Redwood SE), Liam Chen (Redwood SA); Carlos Mendez (MedData CTO), Dr. Anna Li (MedData Lead ML Eng), Samir Patel (Infra Lead), Meera Rao (Product)
summary: Technical deep dive on supporting 128k+ context workflows for MedData Labs use cases (clinical record ingestion, thread-level summaries). topics: KV cache sharding and eviction policies

transcript:
[00:00:00] Jordan (AE): Okay team, thanks for holding this deep dive. The goal is to get into the runtime and perf tradeoffs for 128k-plus contexts. We allocated about an hour.
[00:00:12] Carlos (MedData CTO): Yep, thanks. For background, our LLM product needs to ingest entire patient longitudinal records, sometimes 100k-200k tokens. Latency targets are 1.5s median for summary responses for interactive clinicians, but we're open to batching for offline batch summaries.
[00:00:35] Priya (SE): Got it. Quick clarifying Qs: typical QPS for the interactive path? And are you expecting the entire 128k to be passed as prompt every time or will you use retrieval/chunking?
[00:00:46] Anna (ML Eng): Interactive QPS is low—around 2-5 qps at peak per region—so more latency-sensitive. Batch jobs are hundreds per hour. We plan to use chunking + retrieval but need the model to see the full patient history for global consistency in some ops.
[00:01:05] Liam (SA): Cool. We'll talk through options: full in-memory KV cache with sharding, offload to NVMe with prefetching, and hybrid approaches. Also batching heuristics: continuous batching windows vs immediate small batch for low latency.
[00:01:20] Samir (Infra): On infra constraints—we're hybrid: some PHI must stay in our VPC, some de-identified data can go to a hosted service. We're evaluating Redwood Private (VPC) or on-prem appliance.
[00:01:33] Jordan: Perfect. Let's start with the KV cache. Priya?
[00:01:36] Priya: Sure. For 128k context we can't just blow up the KV cache per request on a single GPU without planning. There are two primary axes: how you're storing kv pairs (sharded per attention head/kv chunk) and eviction/segmenting strategy. For example, we shard KV by layers and sequence slices—so a long seq is sliced in N contiguous windows. We keep hot prefixes in GPU and cold segments in CPU/NVMe with async prefetch.
[00:02:00] Anna: Do you have guidance on how big a 'hot' prefix should be? We observed most user edits are in the recent 8-16k tokens.
[00:02:08] Priya: Exactly; in practice we keep the last 8-32k tokens resident on GPU KV. The rest we either stream in via async prefetch for the generation window or use retrieval to fetch semantically-relevant chunks. That preserves latency for interactive cases while allowing full-document context for batch.
[00:02:25] [crosstalk] Carlos: So if we need a guaranteed 1.5s median, what's feasible?
[00:02:30] Priya: For 1.5s you need the hot prefix on GPU and a model variant tuned for latency—smaller sequence-optimized kernel selection. Also aggressive batching isn't your friend for low qps; continuous batching with very short windows (10-30ms) can help.
[00:02:45] Jordan: On kernels: we validated FlashAttention v2 and some grouped-query attention (GQA) variants. For 128k+ we recommend attention implementations that support block-sparse or tiled attention. FlashAttention gives huge memory perf gains, but you still need careful tiling.
[00:03:02] Priya: Also note some runtime names get munged in transcripts—it's FlashAttention, not 'FlashAttension', and Redwood's runtime will pick kernel at compile time based on seq len and hardware.
[00:03:15] Anna: What about quantization? We need to push cost down.
[00:03:18] Priya: We support 8-bit and 4-bit quantization profiles. 4-bit (narrow fp or GPTQ style) gives big memory wins but can introduce subtle quality regressions on long-context tasks—context retention and name consistency can drift. We recommend running calibration with your prompt sets. For many workloads, mixed precision where activations stay FP16 and weights are 4-bit works well.
[00:03:40] Samir: Does quantization affect KV cache layout?
[00:03:43] Priya: Yes, quantized models reduce KV footprint so more of the context fits in GPU memory. But CPU/NVMe offload paths must decode quantized KV efficiently; otherwise decoding time dominates. Our runtime supports compressed KV blobs and vectorized decode paths.
[00:03:58] [00:04:00] Liam: A big architectural point: for 128k contexts you should consider hierarchical chunking. Two patterns—sliding window overlapping chunks for local context, and a hierarchy where you build condensed summaries of older chunks (a summary index). Retrieval pulls summaries + a few raw chunks. This reduces KV pressure and often preserves global coherence.
[00:04:23] Anna: We were thinking of chunk size 8k with 1k overlap; does that map to your experience?
[00:04:29] Priya: That's reasonable. 8k chunks means ~16 windows for 128k. Overlap of 10-15% helps with boundary effects. For re-ranking, use a lightweight embedding index to pick top 6-10 chunks, then stitch with a synthesis pass. That keeps expensive generation limited to relevant parts.
[00:04:46] Carlos: Any tips on streaming vs full response?
[00:04:48] Priya: For interactive UX, stream token-by-token with early prefix in GPU. If you need deterministic end-to-end with full context, do a single-shot generation but that's higher mem. We often do a hybrid: do an initial draft from hot prefix for fast UI, then spawn a background full-context rerank and update if needed.
[00:05:06] Jordan: Let's talk numbers—throughput and latency examples. Priya, can you give sample perf from our internal runs?
[00:05:12] Priya: On A100 80GB with 4-bit quantized 70B model and a 32k hot prefix + on-demand prefetch, we see ~900-1100 ms median token-latency for a 1k generation window at low QPS. For full 128k full-context single-shot (no retrieval) the end-to-end can be 4-8s depending on how much prefetch is required. These are approximate—your dataset and model matter.
[00:05:36] Anna: For the clinician flow 1.5s median target is tight. So sounds like hybrid approach is best.
[00:05:41] Priya: Right—keep hot prefix on GPU, do retrieval + re-rank from summaries for anything outside hot region. Also tune sampling to reduce token counts.
[00:05:50] Samir: What about storage—do we need NVMe on each GPU node?
[00:05:53] Priya: For prefetching cold KV we recommend NVMe-local cache per node. If you're on Redwood Dedicated, we can provision local NVMe and manage prefetch. For Private/on-prem, we ship prefetch tooling. For strictly air-gapped environments we ship an appliance with NVMe pools.
[00:06:09] Liam: Another point: offloading KV to CPU with high bandwidth RDMA helps, but latency is higher than local NVMe. So if your interactive latency is SLO-critical, local NVMe + hot prefix on GPU is the right call.
[00:06:22] [00:06:25] Carlos: Any special network considerations in VPC?
[00:06:27] Priya: Yes—ensure the cluster's egress rules allow RDMA and that MTU settings support large page transfers. Also KMS traffic (for encryption) should be allowed to your KMS endpoint. For Private deployments, we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and support customer-managed keys.
[00:06:43] Anna: We have HIPAA considerations—do you support audit logs per request and token redaction?
[00:06:49] Jordan: Yes, Redwood Private supports per-request audit logs, token-level cost & latency breakdowns, and integration with customer KMS. We'll share SOC2 artefacts.
[00:06:58] Priya: One more nuance: attention optimization. For 128k you may want to look at sparse attention patterns or combination of local + global tokens (like BigBird-style). Those can reduce quadratic mem growth. We can compile models with custom kernels or use model rewrites to insert efficient attention. But that may change model behavior; require evals.
[00:07:20] Anna: Do you have an eval harness for long context metrics?
[00:07:22] Priya: Yes, Redwood Optimize has a long-context eval harness—we'll run it with your prompts if you share them. It measures coherence, entity consistency, and hallucination rate on long reads.
[00:07:32] [crosstalk] Meera: About cost—how does 4-bit + retrieval compare vs single-shot full 128k?
[00:07:37] Priya: Roughly, blended retrieval + 4-bit quantized synth runs at a fraction of the cost—maybe 30-50% of a naive single-shot end-to-end, depending on retrieval hit rates. The main cost reductions come from smaller working set on the GPU and fewer generation tokens.
[00:07:52] Jordan: OK let's surface typical objections—if MedData wants deterministic outputs, chunking+retrieval can cause non-determinism. Any mitigations?
[00:07:59] Priya: Determinism improves if you keep retrieval stable and use beam or deterministic sampling. Also keep a stable chunking policy and record the retrieval seed. For strict determinism, single-shot with pinned model weights is required, but it's much more expensive.
[00:08:12] Carlos: What about benchmarking—what will you run for us?
[00:08:15] Priya: We'll run: 1) full single-shot 128k generation perf; 2) retrieval+chunking synthetic workload with your prompt distribution; 3) quantized vs fp16 quality checks on your eval set. We'll provide logs, token-level timing, and KV cache hit/miss breakdowns.
[00:08:30] Samir: Any red flags for on-prem?
[00:08:33] Priya: Just hardware sizing—need GPUs with sufficient memory or accelerated NVMe networks and a good orchestration layer. For air-gapped, plan for secure transfer of images and keys. Also network MTU and RDMA config can be fiddly.
[00:08:46] Jordan: Quick recap and next steps?
[00:08:48] Carlos: (brief) Sounds good. We'll assemble a 100MB redacted prompt set and QPS profile.
[00:08:53] Priya: Action: Priya will run internal 128k benchmarks and share runbook and perf traces. Jordan will send pricing and pilot plan. MedData to share constraints and sample prompts.
[00:09:04] [00:09:06] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the benchmark results and schedule the pilot planning. End meeting.
[00:09:14] [end of transcript]
